chapters.title: Chapter 2: How to Actually Buy and Sell Unlisted Shares in India

lessons.title: SEBI and Companies Act Boundaries Every Unlisted-Share Buyer Should Know

children.text: Meena has finally found what looks like a genuine opportunity: an early angel investor in a well-regarded logistics startup wants to sell part of her stake, through a route that checks every box from the previous lesson, a signed SPA, payment to her own account, Form SH-4, the works. Before Meena wires the money, a lawyer friend asks her a different question entirely: has she checked whether the company's own past private placements were done within the law? Meena has no idea what that even means, or why it should matter to her as a buyer, not the company.

body.text: SEBI regulates public markets. For unlisted shares, most of the real legal boundaries come from the Companies Act, 2013, not SEBI, and crossing them can retroactively turn a private deal into a violation, sometimes years after it closes.

children.text: When a company raises money privately, by issuing new shares to a defined group of investors rather than the public at large, it does so under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013. That section allows a private placement to a maximum of 200 persons in a single financial year, not counting qualified institutional buyers or employees receiving shares under an approved ESOP scheme. Cross that number, or advertise the offer widely instead of approaching a defined group directly, and the issue can be treated in law as a deemed public offer, which must then comply with the far stricter disclosure and prospectus requirements of an actual public issue, retroactively.

body.label: The private placement ceiling
body.context: Beyond this (excluding QIBs and ESOP allottees), Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 treats the issue as a deemed public offer, triggering full prospectus-style compliance retroactively.

children.text: Why This Matters Even If You're Just a Buyer

Section 42 binds the company issuing shares, not a later buyer purchasing them in a secondary sale. So why should Meena, who is only buying existing shares from an existing shareholder, care? Because if the company's own original issuance breached the 200-person ceiling or its conditions, that allotment itself can be legally contested. If the shares Meena is buying trace back to a compromised allotment, her own ownership chain is only as solid as that original issuance, however clean her own paperwork with the seller looks.

body.text: Watch for deals structured through a pooled trust, LLP, or similar vehicle designed to let many small buyers collectively invest while appearing, on paper, as a single legal "person" for Section 42 purposes. This kind of structuring has drawn regulatory scrutiny in India, and it adds a layer of legal risk on top of the usual risks of buying unlisted shares.

children.text: Mandatory Demat: A Rule Aimed Directly at You

markDefs.definition: A Companies Act category of company that restricts the transfer of its shares and historically limits its number of shareholders. Most Indian startups incorporate this way initially.

A Companies Act category of company with no cap on shareholder numbers and fewer transfer restrictions than a private limited company. It can be entirely unlisted, and since 2018 must issue and transfer its shares only in dematerialised form.

children.text: Two different "public" ideas get confused constantly in this space. A
is one Companies Act category, restricting share transfers and historically capping shareholder numbers. A

is a different Companies Act category, with no such shareholder cap, and it can be entirely unlisted, never having gone anywhere near a stock exchange. Since 2018, rules under the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 require every unlisted public company to issue and transfer its securities only in dematerialised form. This is exactly why the demat-credit check from the previous lessons matters so much: for an unlisted public company, it is not just good practice, it is the law.

children.text: It is tempting to assume SEBI oversees every share transaction in India. It does not. SEBI's direct jurisdiction is built around the securities market itself: recognised stock exchanges, listed companies, and registered market intermediaries. A private company's internal share transfers generally fall outside that jurisdiction entirely, until the company actually files a Draft Red Herring Prospectus and enters the IPO process, at which point SEBI's Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations take over. For a straightforward secondary sale between two individuals in an unlisted company with no IPO underway, the Companies Act, 2013, administered by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and ordinary contract law are what actually govern the transaction, not SEBI.

body.text: This has a very practical consequence: unlike a trade executed on the NSE through Zerodha, a private unlisted-share deal has no exchange settlement guarantee behind it, no SEBI Investor Protection Fund to fall back on, and generally no SCORES-style regulatory complaint mechanism against the other party. If something goes wrong, your recourse is an ordinary civil or criminal claim, which is slower, costlier, and far less certain than anything a listed-market investor is used to.

body.title: Before Relying on Any Regulatory Protection, Check This
steps: Confirm whether the company is a private limited or public limited company under the Companies Act; this changes whether mandatory demat and other rules apply
Understand that SEBI is generally not your regulator for a private secondary deal; the Companies Act and ordinary contract law are

Ask whether the company's private placement history has stayed within the Section 42 200-person ceiling each financial year; a large cumulative investor base built up over several years is not automatic proof either way
Avoid deals structured through pooled trusts, LLPs, or other vehicles designed to let many small buyers appear as one legal "person"
Do not assume any exchange-style settlement guarantee, investor protection fund, or SEBI complaint mechanism exists for a private unlisted deal

body.label: MCA: Verify a Company's Filings and Compliance History
body.description: Check a company's filing history and compliance record on the MCA portal before relying on any private placement, buyback, or transfer claim a seller or dealer makes.

children.text: Section 68 and Buybacks: A Different Kind of Exit

Not every liquidity event for early investors and employees is an IPO or a secondary sale to an outside buyer. Some companies instead run periodic buybacks under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, where the company itself repurchases shares from existing holders, often specifically to give employees an exit on their ESOP shares without waiting for either an IPO or a secondary buyer. A buyback is capped, standardly, at 25% of the company's paid-up capital plus free reserves in a financial year, and comes with its own procedural conditions.

body.label: Buyback cap
body.context: The standard ceiling under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, on how much of its own equity a company can repurchase in a financial year, subject to further conditions.

children.text: What Actually Happens If the Rules Are Broken

If a company's private placement is found to have breached Section 42, the consequences fall mainly on the company and its officers: it can be forced to refund the entire amount raised, with interest, to every allottee in that placement, on top of separate financial penalties. A buyer in a later secondary sale is not usually the party penalised for the company's original non-compliance. The practical risk for a buyer is different: if the underlying allotment is ever successfully challenged, the shares you bought further down the chain can end up standing on legally uncertain ground, with the burden falling on you to sort it out, not on the company that caused the problem.

body.text: A large cumulative shareholder base built up over several years is not, by itself, proof that a company has breached Section 42. The 200-person cap applies per financial year, not cumulatively across the company's entire history, so a company can add hundreds of small investors over time while staying compliant each year. Treat scale as a reason to ask for compliance confirmation, not as automatic proof of either a violation or a clean record.

body.title: Five Hundred Investors, Five Platforms
body.scenario: Through some casual research, Meena discovers that the logistics startup she is buying into has reportedly sold shares to "over 500 small investors through five different dealer platforms" over the past two years.
body.prompt: What should this tell Meena about the risk here, and what should she actually do next?
body.modelAnswer: 500 investors across two years does not, by itself, mean the company has breached Section 42, since the 200-person cap applies separately to each financial year, not cumulatively over the company's history. It is entirely possible the company stayed within the limit in both years while still ending up with a large investor base overall. What it should do is prompt more diligence, not less: Meena should ask the company's RTA or company secretary to confirm that each year's private placements individually stayed within the Section 42 limits and conditions, check whether any regulator or court has raised concerns about this specific company's placements, and treat a high volume of small-ticket sales through multiple dealers as a signal to look closer, not as either a red flag or a green light on its own.

body.title: Who Actually Governs This Transaction
body.question: Which regulator's rules most directly govern a private secondary sale of shares between two individuals in an unlisted company, with no IPO process underway?
options: SEBI, since it regulates all securities transactions in India
The Companies Act, 2013 (administered by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs), along with ordinary contract law
The Reserve Bank of India, since money is changing hands
The stock exchange where the company might list in future
body.explanation: SEBI's direct jurisdiction generally attaches once a company enters the IPO process or is already listed. A purely private secondary transaction in an unlisted company's shares is chiefly governed by the Companies Act, 2013 and ordinary contract law, not SEBI.

body.title: The Private Placement Ceiling
body.textWithBlank: Under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, a private placement of shares to more than ___ persons in a financial year (excluding qualified institutional buyers and ESOP allottees) risks being treated as a deemed public offer.
body.explanation: The 200-person ceiling applies per financial year. Crossing it, or advertising the offer publicly, exposes the issue to being treated as a deemed public offer with full prospectus-style compliance required retroactively.

body.caption: Where the rules actually come from

cells: How many people can a company privately place shares with in a year?

children.text: The Bottom Line for a Buyer

As a buyer, you are rarely the direct target of a Companies Act compliance breach; those obligations bind the company. But your practical protection in this market comes almost entirely from your own due diligence, not from a regulator standing behind your trade the way SEBI and the exchange stand behind a listed-share purchase. For any meaningful ticket size, involving a company secretary or lawyer to verify the company's compliance history, not just your own transaction's paperwork, is not optional caution. It is the closest thing to a safety net that exists in this market.

body.title: SEBI and Companies Act Boundaries: Key Terms

cards.definition: The Companies Act provision governing private issuance of shares, capping placements at 200 persons per financial year (excluding QIBs and ESOP allottees) before being deemed a public offer.
A private placement that breaches Section 42's limits or conditions, treated in law as if it were a public offer, triggering full prospectus and disclosure requirements retroactively.
The Companies Act provision letting a company repurchase its own shares, capped at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves in a financial year, subject to further conditions.

A company registered as "public" under the Companies Act but not admitted to trading on any stock exchange; subject to mandatory dematerialisation of its shares but not SEBI's listed-company disclosure regime.
SEBI's rules governing the public issue process itself, from DRHP filing through to listing. They generally do not apply to a company's shares until it begins that process.

points: SEBI's direct jurisdiction over a company's shares generally begins only once it enters the IPO process or is already listed. Before that, the Companies Act, 2013, administered by the MCA, is the primary rulebook.

Section 42 caps private placements at 200 persons per financial year (excluding QIBs and ESOP allottees). Breaching it risks a deemed public offer, with refund and penalty consequences for the company.
Unlisted public companies (not private limited ones) must hold and transfer their shares only in dematerialised form, under rules dating to 2018.

A private secondary deal between two individuals has no exchange-style settlement guarantee, no SEBI Investor Protection Fund, and no SCORES-style complaint recourse; ordinary contract law is what you fall back on.

A large cumulative investor base built up over several years does not automatically mean a company has breached Section 42, since the 200-person cap applies per financial year, not cumulatively. Still, it is a reason to ask for compliance confirmation, not to assume either way.
As a buyer, you are rarely the direct target of a Companies Act compliance breach, but a contested or void allotment upstream can still leave your own ownership on shaky ground.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal advice. Meena is fictional and used purely for illustration. Company law and SEBI regulations referenced here, including thresholds and caps, are subject to amendment; always verify current provisions with a qualified company secretary or lawyer, and review the company's actual compliance history, before relying on any of them in a real transaction.
